transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-11
Start time (UTC): 15:00
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Novara PM), Carlos Mendes (Novara Backend), Aisha Brown (Novara Sec)

Summary:
Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming behavior, key generation parameters (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), and recommended retry/backoff patterns. Customer emphasized latency sensitivity for live triage flows and security/compliance needs (KMS, retention). Decided to proceed with sandbox POC and share security pack.

Topics Covered:
- Hosted Chat Quickstart and Console tour
- Streaming semantics and how to stitch partial deltas
- Parameter guidance (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop) and practical defaults
- Retry/backoff strategies, idempotency and client-side reconnect patterns
- Cost levers: batching, cache hints, token budgeting and Optimize recommendations
- Security: KMS, audit logs, SOC2 scope, VPC/dedicated options

Action items (recorded in transcript):
- Maya to send SOC2 + security whitepaper and KMS integration notes
- Liam to drop sandbox notebook and streaming client example
- Novara (Carlos) to provide traffic profile and prompt set for benchmarking

Questions raised:
- "How much does streaming lower perceived latency vs non-streaming?"
- "What happens when a stream disconnects mid-response?"
- "Can we pin a model with a rollout policy and automatic fallback to a quantized variant?"

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm Maya with Redwood, quick intro — liam is our solutions engineer, we'll do a short demo of hosted chat and then leave time for Qs.
[00:18] Priya Singh: thanks, we only have 45 minutes, super focused on latency and cost tradeoffs for our triage assistant.
[00:30] Liam O'Connor: perfect, we'll surface live latency numbers and then show retry patterns — first slide is a 2-minute console tour, then a code walk.
[01:05] Carlos Mendes: quick note, our infra is in GCP europe-west, typical request rate is 60 req/s during peaks, p95 latency target is 300ms for initial tokens.
[01:35] Aisha Brown: security is big for us — are you SOC2 type II? what about KMS integration and retention windows?
[01:50] Maya Chen: yes SOC2 available, we'll share certs after; KMS supported for Private/Dedicated, hosted can use customer-managed keys through our partner setup, we'll attach docs.
[02:20] Liam O'Connor: jumping into the console — here is model catalog, you can pick a curated model, the console shows verified perf numbers, and the right-hand panel has recommended params for low-latency interactive use.
[03:05] Liam O'Connor: showing streaming sample, note how we stream token deltas to the client, you stitch them and render progressively — perceived latency drops because user sees first tokens quickly.
[03:40] Priya Singh: is that SSE or websockets? what's client best practice?
[03:50] Liam O'Connor: we support streaming over server-sent events and websocketized clients, code sample in the sandbox uses EventSource; reconnect logic should be idempotent- aware, include request id and partial response cursor if you want resume.
[04:25] Carlos Mendes: what if the stream dies mid-response — our UX needs to recover gracefully without duplication.
[04:40] Liam O'Connor: good question — pattern we recommend: client keeps a request-id, on reconnect you call a resume endpoint with last token idx (or just re-request with the same id) server-side will dedupe if request was fully persisted; otherwise we provide deterministic retry with a short tail. there is slight variance across model families but runtime provides a resume token and KV cache snapshot on dedicated/private.
[05:20] Priya Singh: K V cash? (laughter) sorry, k v cache. sometimes the transcript spells it wrong.
[05:35] Maya Chen: yeah kv cache, not cash :) quick note on params: for triage we recommend temperature 0.0-0.2, top_p 0.8-1.0, and a max_token cap of 100 to keep costs predictable.
[06:05] Liam O'Connor: we also show a token budget in the console per-route — you can enforce soft caps and fallbacks to a cheaper smaller model if budget is exceeded.
[06:35] Carlos Mendes: how about batching — we have bursts, can we batch without adding latency?
[06:45] Liam O'Connor: batching is workload dependent; for live interactive you want small batch windows (10-50ms) or continuous batching. our runtime does automatic continuous batching and you can tune the tradeoff with a latency SLO slider.
[07:10] Priya Singh: any tip on quantization or Optimize recommendations?
[07:20] Maya Chen: Optimize will analyze your sample prompts and suggest model variants, quantization levels, and expected unit cost delta — it's an ops report we can run against your prompt set.
[07:40] Aisha Brown: On retention, hosted keeps logs for X days by default, is that configurable? we need 90 days for auditing.
[07:55] Maya Chen: default is 30, enterprise plans can extend to 90+ and include longer trace retention; also audit logs and per-token breakdown tied to route IDs.
[08:20] Liam O'Connor: moving to demo code — here's a simple streaming client in node, you create a session, send messages, then listen for data events. important: include an idempotency_key header to avoid double billing on retries and use exponential backoff for 429s.
[09:05] Liam O'Connor: demo shows a reconnect where we lost connectivity at ~[09:30], then resume flow recovers without showing duplicate final answer — this uses our resume token.
[10:00] Priya Singh: are 429s usually spikes or sustained?
[10:10] Liam O'Connor: often spikes during bursts; we expose quota and capacity routing — you can set a reserved dedicated pool if you need firm SLOs. hosted has soft fallbacks: route to cheaper variant or queue.
[10:45] Carlos Mendes: can we pin model versions? we need deterministic outputs for compliance.
[10:55] Maya Chen: yes, pin model version and pin rollout policy; you can also pin a quantized variant for cost. console lets you configure canary rollouts and automatic fallback to a stable variant.
[11:25] Aisha Brown: encryption at rest and in transit?
[11:33] Maya Chen: everything TLS in transit, at-rest encryption with provider-managed keys, and customer-managed keys for Dedicated/Private — we'll include KMS guide.
[12:00] Liam O'Connor: quick aside on token accounting — we walked through how prompt vs completion tokens count, and how to trim system prompts, use stop tokens to avoid over-generation, plus pre-tokenization heuristics.
[12:45] Priya Singh: can we run a latency benchmark with our payloads?
[12:52] Maya Chen: yes, that's part of the POC — we ask you provide 1000 representative prompts and we'll run a perf sweep across models and quant levels.
[13:15] Carlos Mendes: what about throttling behavior and retries strategy example?
[13:25] Liam O'Connor: recommended client-side: on 429/503 do exponential backoff with jitter (start 100ms, cap 2s, 4-5 retries), on connection reset attempt resume or gracefully re-request — importantly include idempotency_key to avoid duplicate effects server-side.
[14:05] Priya Singh: any guidance for streaming partial credit — like optimistic display then finalize?
[14:15] Liam O'Connor: yes, render partial deltas but mark as provisional until final event; have the client replace provisional text on finalization to avoid showing contradictions.
[14:40] Maya Chen: quick console tour again — Optimize tab suggests batch sizes, quant profiles per-model, and shows estimated unit cost — you can export recommendations.
[15:10] Carlos Mendes: can Optimize integrate into our CI to block regressions?
[15:20] Maya Chen: yes, you can publish prompt sets and evals, Optimize will run regression checks and alert on quality drop and token cost regressions.
[15:50] Aisha Brown: for POC, we want to demo SOC2 and KMS, and see a latency run. timeline?
[16:00] Maya Chen: propose POC kickoff Oct 18, 2-week scope: onboarding, perf runs, and a short UX smoke test. we'll provide sandbox creds and a sample streaming client.
[16:18] Priya Singh: sounds good, any blockers on our side?
[16:25] Carlos Mendes: we'll need a small token to access sandbox from GCP, and a sample traffic sketch which we'll provide.
[17:00] Liam O'Connor: logging and traces — we'll show token-level latency and per-route breakdowns in the console; you can add tracing hooks to map requests to backend traces.
[17:35] Priya Singh: about price — ballpark? nothing final but we need to understand unit economics.
[17:45] Maya Chen: we'll send a usage-based estimate and a dedicated pool quote if required; pricing doc coming with SOC2 pack.
[18:05] Carlos Mendes: any competitors we should consider? we've looked at OpenAI and Anthropic for model fidelity.
[18:20] Maya Chen: yep common; we differentiate on production controls, predictable cost levers and private/dedicated deployment options.
[18:40] Priya Singh: last question on rate limits and bursts — what happens to queued requests?
[18:52] Liam O'Connor: hosted will queue for short bursts, or return 429 if exceeded — you can configure soft quotas and reserved capacity on Dedicated.
[19:15] Maya Chen: ok quick recap: Maya sends SOC2 and pricing, Liam drops sandbox and streaming notebook, Novara sends traffic profile and prompt set, we aim to kickoff Oct 18.
[19:40] Priya Singh: thanks, that works.
[19:45] Aisha Brown: thanks everyone.
[19:50] Maya Chen: we'll follow up with calendar invite for kickoff, and include the POC runbook and success criteria doc.
[20:05] END OF RECORDING

Notes: transcript has occasional mis-hearings and filler words; speaker labels inferred from calendar and may be slightly off in places.
